# ACT Math Formulas: 40+ Must-Know Equations (2026 Guide)


## TL;DR


The ACT does not provide a formula sheet, so every math formula must come from memory. This guide covers 40+ formulas organized by topic and ranked by how often they appear on the 2026 Enhanced ACT. Algebra and geometry formulas alone cover roughly 70% of the math section. Focus your memorization there first, then layer in coordinate geometry, trigonometry, and the rare advanced formulas only if you’re chasing a top score.


---


The Enhanced ACT gives you 45 math questions in 50 minutes. That’s about 67 seconds per question. There is no formula sheet. Unlike the digital SAT, which hands you a reference sheet of geometry formulas, the ACT expects everything to come from your head.


This matters more now than it used to. On the Enhanced ACT (the only version available as of 2026), Math is one of just three scored sections, meaning it accounts for 33% of your Composite score instead of the old 25%. A weak math section hurts more than ever.


Below is every ACT math formula worth memorizing, grouped by topic and ranked by how frequently each one actually shows up on test day. If you want to build a study plan around these formulas,[explore ACT prep options](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/prep) that include diagnostics and targeted practice.


> **What Math Formulas Do You Need to Know for the ACT?**
>
>
> The ACT does not provide a general math formula sheet, so students should memorize the essential formulas before test day. The most useful formulas cover algebra, geometry, coordinate geometry, trigonometry, statistics, and probability. Start with the quadratic formula, slope formula, exponent rules, Pythagorean theorem, area and volume formulas, and basic trigonometric ratios. Then review less common topics, such as logarithms, matrices, and combinations, based on your strengths and target score.
>
>
> Use this guide as a reference: learn what each formula means, practice recognizing when to apply it, and solve timed questions to build recall.

No. The ACT does not provide any formula reference. This is the single biggest difference between ACT math and SAT math for students deciding between the two tests.

The ACT also tests topics the SAT skips entirely: logarithms, matrices, law of sines and cosines, and more trigonometry. If you’re weighing which test to take, our[SAT vs ACT comparison](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/sat-vs-act-key-differences-how-to-choose) breaks down the full picture.


One reassurance: if a question requires a truly obscure formula, the ACT typically provides it within the problem itself. You won’t need to memorize the volume of an oblate spheroid. But the standard formulas below? Those are on you.

## ACT Math Content Breakdown


The Enhanced ACT Math section contains 45 questions to be completed in 50 minutes. The official content framework groups higher-level math into five reporting categories: Number & Quantity, Algebra, Functions, Geometry, and Statistics & Probability. It also assesses essential skills and mathematical modeling.


Here is the official distribution for the higher-math reporting categories:


Reporting category


Approximate share


Number & Quantity


10–12%


Algebra


17–20%


Functions


17–20%


Geometry


17–20%


Statistics & Probability


12–15%


The ACT also reports Integrating Essential Skills as approximately 20% and Modeling as at least 20%. These are overlapping reporting dimensions, so they should not be added to the five categories as if all percentages represented separate portions of the test.


For studying, use these categories as a guide rather than a guarantee of how many questions will test a specific formula. Your best priorities are to master foundational algebra, functions, geometry, and essential arithmetic skills before spending extensive time on less familiar advanced topics.


**Important:** Coordinate geometry is not a separate official reporting category in this framework. Its skills overlap with algebra, functions, and geometry.

### Concepts That Replace Formulas


Here’s a memorization shortcut that practitioners on Reddit and prep forums frequently recommend. Some “formulas” are really just concepts:


**Perimeter** is not a formula you need to memorize separately for each shape. Perimeter just means “add up all the sides.” Whether it’s a triangle, rectangle, pentagon, or irregular polygon, you’re doing the same thing. PrepScholar makes this same point: understanding a concept can eliminate the need to memorize multiple formulas.


**Surface area** works similarly. It’s the total area of all the faces of a 3D shape. If you can find the area of each face and add them up, you don’t strictly need the surface area formulas above (though knowing them saves time).

## Coordinate Geometry Formulas


Coordinate geometry covers about 7 questions. These formulas connect algebra to the coordinate plane.


Formula


Expression


Priority


Distance formula


d = √\[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²\]


Must Know


Midpoint formula


M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)


Must Know


Equation of a circle


(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²


Should Know


Equation of an ellipse


(x − h)²/a² + (y − k)²/b² = 1


Good to Know


The distance formula is just the Pythagorean theorem in disguise. If you forget it, draw a right triangle on the coordinate plane, find the horizontal and vertical legs, and apply a² + b² = c². Same answer.


The equation of a circle typically appears as just one question per test. The center is (h, k) and the radius is r. Watch for the signs: (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25 means the center is (3, −2) and the radius is 5.


### Desmos and Coordinate Geometry


If you’re taking the digital ACT, you get access to a built-in Desmos graphing calculator during the math section. This changes the game for coordinate geometry. Desmos can graph circle equations, find intersections of lines, and solve systems of equations visually. You still need to recognize what equation form you’re looking at, but the computation side gets easier.


Note that Desmos is only available on the digital ACT. Paper test-takers need their own approved calculator. And the ACT’s version of Desmos disables some advanced functions (sec, cot, arcsec, statistical functions like mad and cov), so don’t count on it for trigonometry shortcuts. For more on graphing calculator strategy, our[Desmos tips for the SAT](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/desmos) covers transferable techniques.

Median and mode aren’t really “formulas” but rather concepts. Median is the middle value after sorting. Mode is whichever value appears most often. The ACT tests these almost every time.


Combinations and permutations are rare, probably appearing on one test out of three. The key distinction: combinations are for when order doesn’t matter (choosing a committee), permutations are for when order matters (assigning first, second, third place).

## How to Memorize ACT Math Formulas


Knowing which formulas exist is step one. Actually remembering them under pressure is step two. Here’s what works.


### Prioritize by Frequency


PrepScholar puts it well: “Sometimes you don’t have the time to memorize all formulas, and that’s OK. You can still be well-prepared for the majority of math questions by memorizing half or even fewer.”


The algebra and geometry formulas tagged “Must Know” above cover approximately 70% of the math section. Start there. If you only have two weeks, that’s where your time goes.


### Learn Concepts Where Possible


Not every formula needs to be memorized as a formula. The perimeter example is the clearest case: instead of memorizing separate perimeter formulas for rectangles, triangles, and parallelograms, just remember that perimeter means “add all the sides.” Surface area works the same way: “add the areas of all the faces.”


This concept-over-formula approach reduces your memorization load while actually improving your flexibility on unfamiliar shapes.


### Use Spaced Repetition


Flashcards work, but only if you space them out. Review new formulas daily for the first week, then every other day, then twice a week. Apps like Anki automate this. The goal is to move formulas from short-term to long-term memory before test day.


### Practice Under Timed Conditions


Memorizing a formula in your bedroom is different from recalling it with a clock ticking. Practitioners on r/ACT consistently recommend “spamming problem sets” as the best way to cement formulas. The act of retrieving a formula under time pressure builds the kind of recall you need on test day.[ACT practice tests](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/practice-tests) that simulate real timing are the best way to test whether your memorization is holding up.


### Know Your Score Target


If you’re aiming for a 25, the “Must Know” and “Should Know” formulas are enough. The advanced formulas (logarithms, matrices, law of cosines) matter only if you’re pushing for 30+. Students who reported scores in the 33-36 range on r/ACT generally say they had every formula on this page committed to memory, but they also spent months building that foundation.


Wondering where you currently stand? The[ACT score predictor](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/predictor) can help you identify which categories need the most attention.

The goal is not simply to recite equations. It is to recognize the right formula, apply it accurately, and solve the problem within the available time.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Does the ACT give you a formula sheet?


No. The ACT does not provide any formula reference sheet. The SAT provides a short geometry reference, but the ACT expects every formula to come from memory. If a question requires an unusually advanced formula, it will typically be given within the question itself.


### How many formulas do you need for the ACT?


About 30 to 40 core formulas cover the vast majority of questions. The “Must Know” tier (roughly 20 formulas) handles about 70% of the math section. Add the “Should Know” tier and you’re prepared for nearly everything.


### What is the most important ACT math formula?


The Pythagorean theorem (a² + b² = c²) is arguably the most tested single formula. Close runners-up include the slope formula, the quadratic formula, and the area formulas for triangles and circles. These five formulas alone touch dozens of questions across the test.


### Are ACT math formulas the same as SAT formulas?


There’s significant overlap in algebra and geometry, but the ACT tests additional topics the SAT does not cover at all: trigonometric identities and graphs, logarithms, matrices, law of sines, and law of cosines.


### Has the Enhanced ACT changed which formulas I need?


The format changed (45 questions in 50 minutes, 4 answer choices, Math is 33% of Composite), but the math content itself hasn’t shifted. You still need the same formulas. The stakes are just higher per question because each one represents a larger share of your score.


### Can Desmos replace formula memorization on the digital ACT?


Partially. The built-in Desmos calculator on the digital ACT can graph functions, find intersections, and solve systems visually. This reduces your reliance on some coordinate geometry and algebra computations. But Desmos won’t help with most geometry, trigonometry identities, or logarithm rules. It’s a tool, not a substitute for knowing your formulas.


### How should I study ACT math formulas if I only have two weeks?


Focus exclusively on the “Must Know” formulas in algebra and geometry. Use flashcards with spaced repetition, and spend most of your time doing timed practice problems rather than just reviewing the formula list. Applying formulas under time pressure is what builds real recall.


### Is it worth memorizing logarithm and matrix formulas?


Only if you’re aiming for a 30+ score. Logarithm questions appear once or twice per test, and matrix questions are even rarer. If you’re feeling overwhelmed, skip these and lock down the high-frequency formulas first.


### How many math formulas should I memorize for the ACT?


There is no official number of formulas every student must memorize. Start with foundational algebra, geometry, coordinate geometry, and trigonometry formulas, then review statistics, probability, and other topics covered by the test. Focus on understanding when and how to apply each formula instead of memorizing a fixed number without practicing.


### What is the hardest ACT math formula to remember?


There is no single hardest formula for every student. Some students struggle with the quadratic formula, trigonometric identities, or the laws of sines and cosines, while others find coordinate geometry more challenging. Identify your weak areas through practice questions and prioritize formulas you frequently forget or apply incorrectly.


### Can I pass ACT Math without memorizing every formula?


You do not need to memorize every mathematical formula that could possibly appear in a problem. The ACT provides formulas within certain questions when a complex or unfamiliar relationship is required. However, you should know foundational formulas and concepts well enough to recognize common problem types and solve them efficiently. The ACT does not provide a general math formula sheet.
